top_cited_works.title: Mitigation of Plume-Surface Interaction Effects via Landing Mats.
top_cited_works.abstract: The potential of regolith-based landing mats to mitigate the adverse effects of operating rocket-based propulsive systems near unconsolidated granular surfaces is studied in a sub-scale cold flow plume-surface interactions (PSI) facility. The ejecta cloud and surface crater produced by an underexpanded sonic jet directly impinging on a granular media bed are compared to those in the presence of a landing mat above the granular surface. Mats with varying diameters are investigated under the same plume characteristics using a converging nozzle at a pressure ratio of 2.96 discharging at atmospheric conditions, and at a nozzle exit plane to surface distance of 20 nozzle diameters, De. Glass particles of about 100 micrometers in diameter are used as granular simulant. The landing mats, when not completely perforated by the impinging jet, reduce the pressure at the surface, which is quantified in separate experiments using an instrumented impingement plate. Post-test X-ray micro-CT imaging is used to characterize the mats before and after jet impingement. top_cited_works.title: Ejecta Tracking During Plume-Surface Interactions at Sub-Atmospheric Conditions
top_cited_works.abstract: The thruster plume of a lunar or Martian lander necessarily impinges on and interacts with the regolith surface during landing. Regolith is lofted and ejected from the surface, which results in a crater at the landing site. The dynamics of this process are not well understood. The work reported here explores the velocity (both magnitude and direction) of ejecta particles in a sub-scale experiment with a Mach 5 cold-gas nitrogen jet impinging on a bed of glass microspheres. The ejected particle velocity is measured using a planar laser PTV system with four high-speed cameras and studied as a function of the jet nozzle altitude above the surface. Results show that, as nozzle altitude decreases, the initial burst of ejected particles has larger speeds and a steeper (more vertical) ejection angle for both lunar and Martian ambient conditions. At low altitudes, particles ejecting at steeper angles between 40 and 50 degrees move at speeds up to 15 m/s faster than those traveling close to the surface between 0 and 10 degrees. Results also show that during tests with Martian ambient conditions, ejection speeds are slower by up to 10 m/s than tests done with lunar ambient pressures.

top_cited_works.title: Data-driven Framework to Characterize Crater Dynamics During Plume-Surface Interactions
top_cited_works.abstract: During propulsive landings on the Moon, Mars, or other terrestrial bodies, high-speed thruster plumes erode the regolith surface, generating ejecta that lift off and pose hazards to the vehicle and surroundings. The volume and shape of craters formed during plume-surface interactions (PSI) depend on thruster characteristics, ambient conditions, and regolith properties. We review existing analytical, empirical, and data-driven models of plume-induced granular erosion, highlighting the need for models that accurately capture PSI across a broader range of conditions. In this work, low-pressure, high-speed data from NASA’s Physics-Focused Ground Test (PFGT) campaign were used to characterize crater evolution and morphology across varying nozzle mass flow rates, nozzle heights, background pressures, and regolith simulants. Half-space experiments employed a splitter plate aligned with the nozzle axis, enabling high-speed recordings of crater formation. Crater profiles were extracted using an in-house image processing tool, augmented with an open-source machine learning algorithm.
